chapter_theme: Civakan's companions, searching for him, tell an ascetic mother in the hermitage that he was seized for death; her lament reveals that she is Vijayai, the dead king's queen, and Civakan his heir, and she charges them in secret to bring him to her, while they vow to crush the usurper.

1797.reading: A friend begins his report: Civakan, the strong-bowed first son taken up by Kantukkatan, the old merchant chief of the city, who ends the grief of all who think of him, was one day, for a fault, seized by the king.
1797.event: Civakan's companion tells Vijayai that the king seized Civakan for an offence.
1797.nuance: The speaker calls Civakan என் தோழன் and names the foster father, not the true one: he does not yet know whose son he is talking to. Who the king is (Kattiyangaran) is left to the story so far; the fault (தவறு) is not named here.

1798.reading: The friend says the king had Civakan's bangled shoulders bound tight to be killed in the city of bannered mansions while the women wept, and the mother, stricken, falls like a hooded snake struck by thunder.
1798.event: Hearing that Civakan was bound to be put to death, Vijayai falls senseless.
1798.nuance: Line 4's வீழ்ந்தாள் shifts from the friend's report to the narrator's, so the verse carries both voices; the falling woman is named only in later verses.

1799.reading: On hearing the harm that came to the young lord, the ascetic women of the great hermitage, their eyes rolling, are shaken as though it were harm to their own dear son and fall, and those present say that women indeed have great compassion.
1799.event: The ascetic women fall in grief as if Civakan were their own son.
1799.nuance: Who falls and who speaks the closing words (என்றார்) is not stated; reading the fallers as the hermitage women and the speakers as the onlookers is a guess from line 1's மாதவப் பெருமை and line 3's தம் மகனுக்கு.

1800.reading: They seek a fit remedy to quench the great queen's swoon and revive her with water thick with ground sandal, and she of the lute-like voice, unable to bear it, faints again and begins to lament.
1800.event: Vijayai is revived with sandal water, faints again and laments.
1800.nuance: The narrator gives her the title மாபெருந் தேவி, the queen's rank she has hidden in the hermitage, just before the friends learn it.

1801.reading: Vijayai cries that when the guardian fell amid his sea-wide army and she rode the false peacock to the burning ground and fell there, he, her lord, appeared as her companion, and asks whether he now hides from her.
1801.event: Vijayai recalls the king's death, her flight on the mechanical peacock and her son's birth at the burning ground.
1801.nuance: She calls the newborn எம்மானே and her companion (துணையாகி): the child born in the cremation ground is remembered as the one who stood by her there, and his reported death as his hiding from her (ஒளித்தியோ), the word the dead king's women used of him.

1802.reading: She laments that Kantukkatan, with his bright spear, carried the child off in joy and gave him to his wife, and that Sunandai who reared him without tiring is now struck by this harm, crying 'my lord' again and again because he has gone.
1802.event: Vijayai recalls the merchant taking the child to his wife Sunandai, who raised him.
1802.nuance: Line 3 நையாள் வளர்த்த சுநந்தை நவையுற வென் divides doubtfully; whether the harm is said to fall on Sunandai or on the speaker turns on it.

1803.reading: She says the three dreams the spear-bearing king once spoke of were the raft on which she bore her life, and now her king has died without hearing her cry, and that raft has failed her.
1803.event: Vijayai says the king's reading of her three dreams kept her alive and has now failed.
1803.nuance: முன்னுரைத்த points back to the king's reading of her dreams before Civakan's birth; she held to the promise of the son's crown and did not let herself weigh the falling tree he would not explain. என்னரசே here addresses the son, the king the dream promised.

1804.reading: She says that hoping to become the king's mother and see him guard the people under his umbrella, she has done only sin; she had thought that when her care was over he would bid her go and she would go, but he has gone before her.

claims.claim: her loss is the fruit of the sin she herself has done

1804.nuance: Line 1 கோவமா வாகி is hard to divide (கோ அம்மா ஆகி, 'becoming the king's mother', is one guess), and the sense of the whole verse turns on it. The grief is the reversal of the order of deaths: a mother expected to be sent off by her son.

1805.reading: She calls him son of the king, bull of war of the Kuru line, lord of Emamangatham, her dear life, a Kama, and says she has wrecked her ship in the sea, and asks whether he will go without seeing her tears.
1805.nuance: In grief she says aloud what she has kept hidden: the titles கோமான் மகனே, குருகுலத்தார் போரேறே and ஏமாங்கதத்தார் இறைவா tell the listening friends that Civakan is the dead king's son.

1806.reading: She says that hearing from those who came that the king's son was unharmed, she stayed hidden and grieved many times, and now she wastes away with this sorrow, crying 'alas, Aram, I cannot bear it'.
1806.event: Vijayai tells how she lived hidden, content with reports of her son's safety.
1806.nuance: She addresses அறனே directly, as if the moral order owed her the son for whose sake she stayed hidden. Her concealment (மறைந்திருந்து) was the deity's counsel at the birth.

1807.reading: She says she once saw her son and her eyes were cooled, but the hope of seeing him once more has failed, and cries that no women like her should be born in this world; then the one with the gait of a hen-swan falls like a peacock.
1807.event: Vijayai ends her lament and falls senseless again.
1807.nuance: Line 2 பிழைத்ததென் றேவிர்கா divides doubtfully; reading ஏவிர்காள் as a call to the women around her is a guess. The wish that no woman like her be born turns her grief into a judgement on her own birth.

1808.reading: Hearing the words of the queen of the garlanded king who shamed the battle elephants, the friends, hearts brimming, sigh hotly and look into one another's faces with eyes full of tears.
1808.event: The friends realise from her lament that Vijayai is the dead king's queen and Civakan his son.
1808.nuance: The recognition is wordless: they look at each other's faces. The narrator gives her the title பெருமாட்டி of the king, the knowledge they have just gained.

1809.reading: Saying 'see how the deed has ripened', the friends wave their hands with bright bracelets and rise and dance for joy, saying that a life has come into being that will be Death to the base man who seized the sea-girt land.
1809.event: The friends rejoice that Civakan is the rightful heir who will destroy the usurper.

claims.claim: a deed ripens and brings its fruit to the doer
the usurper who seized the land will meet his death through the rightful heir

1809.nuance: கருமம் விளைந்தவாறு can be read as the usurper's deed ripening against him or as the fortune now ripening for Civakan; either way the friends read the queen's secret as fate's work. Their joy follows straight on her grief, since they know what she does not, that Civakan lives.

1810.reading: As Vijayai lies fallen like a peacock, they bend over her and do many cooling things, and when she of wide spear-split eyes rises lamenting, they surround her, bow and worship and tell her how it stands with him.
1810.event: The friends revive Vijayai, bow to her and begin to tell her what became of Civakan.
1810.nuance: They now bow and worship (தொழுது இறைஞ்சி) the woman they had addressed as a hermitage mother: the recognition changes their bearing before it changes their words.

1811.reading: The friends tell her that when he neared the execution ground a deity took him, saying 'this is a deity's station', and when it removed him he went, and the young man now rejoices like a tusker calf joined with a well-marked young she-elephant among the herds of the hills.
1811.event: The friends tell Vijayai that a deity carried Civakan from the execution ground and that he now lives happily with a wife.
1811.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (கொண்டொர் தெய்வத / நிலைக்கள மிதுவென) divide doubtfully, so what the deity is said to have declared is unsure. The friends know only that a deity took him; the story told earlier, of the dog he once helped returning as a god, is not in their account.

1812.reading: The friends say that the garlanded one, putting off his disguise, will now take on being the great son who owns the kingship, and that they have come and bowed at her red feet; she of the mango-slice eyes, rejoicing within, speaks.
1812.event: The friends promise that Civakan will claim his kingship, and Vijayai, glad, begins to answer.
1812.nuance: போர்வை, 'the covering', is his life as a merchant's son: the friends treat the foster identity as a cloak to be thrown off now the birth is known.

1813.reading: Vijayai says that the guardian of the earth called Saccandan, born under Bharani, who stood unguarded against all his foes, met the end Hiranya met through the love he kept fixed on her.
1813.event: Vijayai tells the friends who Civakan's father was and how he died.

claims.claim: the king fell because of his love for his queen

1813.nuance: பகை யாவையு / மரணி லானென்கட் divides doubtfully (அரண் இலான், 'without defence', is one reading). She blames her husband's death on his love for her, the cause the councillors had named. The comparison with இரணியன் draws on a Vaishnava story in a Jain epic, used only as a figure for a sudden violent death.

1814.reading: She says that they should tell Nambi in order all the evil she, Vijayai, whose name went through the world and who is now without glory, suffered when her lord died through his attachment, and bring the young lord to her without fail.
1814.event: Vijayai asks the friends to tell Civakan her story and bring him to her.
1814.nuance: பசையி னாற்றுஞ்சி may mean the king died of attachment or that she lay in it; the verse's account of her suffering turns on it.

1815.reading: She tells them to speak of this matter to no one but Nambi and to trust no one, and, since harm comes in such ways, not to talk with fools or with women.
1815.event: Vijayai charges the friends to keep Civakan's birth secret.

claims.claim: in danger, trust no one with a secret
a secret must not be spoken to fools or to women

1815.nuance: A woman who has hidden her own rank for years bars women from the secret; the warning falls on her own sex.

1816.reading: She says that the hearts of enemies, the track of a snake, the hearts of girdled women and lightning in the high cloud do not go straight, and tells the men of smoking spears to go on their way guarding themselves.

claims.claim: women's hearts, like enemies' hearts, do not run straight

1816.nuance: The list sets women's hearts among things whose course cannot be predicted, next to enemies and snakes; the speaker is the epic's model of the faithful wife, so the maxim is offered as prudence, not grievance.

1817.reading: The friends promise that within one month they will bring the man of the unbending bow to her virtuous feet and then do as she commands and crush the enemy at the root, and she, like a jewelled creeper soiled, tells them to resolve on that.
1817.event: The friends vow to bring Civakan to his mother within a month, and Vijayai approves.
1817.nuance: The vow sets a term (ஒருமதி எல்லை) the story will have to keep, and the mother's command, not Civakan's, is to start the war on the usurper.

1818.reading: Bowing their heads at the feet of Vijayai of close penance, who fasted with her senses held tight and kept a flawless rule of life, they return to the fragrant grove, eat the food they wish and order the army to rise, and the conches rise roaring.
1818.event: The friends take leave of Vijayai, eat in the grove and set the army marching.
1818.nuance: பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று gives the widow's life in the hermitage the language of ascetic sense-restraint, in the verse that sends out an army at her command.

1819.reading: At the din of the golden bells of the horses leaping skyward, a peacock that had caught a red velvet-mite and was preening its feathers looks like silk-clad women who, abashed, their coral lips shining, draw back their hair and wipe away its redness.
1819.nuance: The image of shy women wiping away red closes a chapter that has just warned against women's hearts.

links.note: In 225 the king reads the dream's crown as her son and leaves the falling tree unexplained; here she says that reading was the raft that kept her alive.
links.teaches: The half-told dream reading the epic first showed as the king's tact becomes, years later, the single hope a widow lived by, so the omitted part of the omen proves the part she could not afford to hear.

links.note: At the burning ground in 309 she asked the newborn whether this was how kings are born; here she remembers that same birth as the son appearing as her companion.
links.teaches: The birth among corpses, first lamented as a disgrace to a king's son, is remembered as rescue, and the loss she now fears is told as the loss of that companion of the cremation ground.

links.note: In 260 the councillor says the king will be killed by Death, by the woman and by his own fault; here the queen says he died through the love he fixed on her.
links.teaches: The cause the councillor named in passing, the woman, is accepted by the woman herself, so the epic's verdict on the king's fall is confirmed by the one it blamed rather than by the narrator.

links.note: At the birth the deity foretold that the boy would crush the king who stood against him; here the friends, learning his birth, hail him as the life that will be Death to the usurper.
links.teaches: A prophecy spoken only to a hidden mother passes, through her grief, into the mouths of armed men, which is how the epic moves a foretold fate from secret knowledge to a plan of war.

links.note: The proverb says one's suffering is one's own old deed and the foe only the sent servant; the friends see the usurper's deed ripen and the heir become its agent of Death.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show the sent-servant idea from both ends: the proverb tells the sufferer not to rage at the agent, while the epic shows men rejoicing to become the agent of another's ripened deed.

gains.a: the friends' cry gains a stated account of how a ripened deed uses a human hand, which explains why they can call Civakan Death without calling him the cause
gains.b: the proverb's consoling rule gains a scene from the agent's side, where the instrument of the deed is glad and armed, which the proverb never considers

links.note: The Kural forbids trusting anyone unexamined but bids trust after examination; Vijayai bids the friends trust no one at all with the secret except Civakan.
links.teaches: The Kural's two-step rule of trust assumes time to examine people, and the epic shows a mother hiding an heir from a usurper dropping the second step altogether, so that danger turns examined trust into blanket silence.

gains.a: Vijayai's charge gains a rule against which its absoluteness can be measured, showing how far beyond ordinary prudence her fear has pushed her
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its own first clause, தேறற்க யாரையும், is held without the second, marking the limit of the time to examine it presumes

links.note: The Naladiyar's eel-like doubleness belongs to women who sell intimacy; Vijayai, the faithful queen, puts the hearts of girdled women in general among things that do not go straight.
links.teaches: The quatrain confines double dealing to a class of women and blames the men who embrace them, whereas the epic's chaste widow extends the suspicion to all women when a secret is at stake, so the pair shows the charge widening from a trade to a sex.

gains.a: the queen's maxim gains a narrower ethical source, which shows how much she generalises the doubleness the moral books assigned to courtesans
gains.b: the quatrain gains a woman speaker who uses its suspicion as practical counsel, testing whether its warning was about trade or about women

links.note: The Kural praises those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses; the epic gives Vijayai that sense-restraint (பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று) in the verse that sends an army out at her word.
links.teaches: The couplet makes quenching the senses the way to a long, settled life, while the epic shows the same restraint in a widow who still commands a war of revenge, so ascetic control of the senses is shown sitting with, not ending, worldly purpose.

gains.a: Vijayai's penance gains the weight of the Kural's opening ideal, so her austerity reads as the highest discipline and not mere widowhood
gains.b: the couplet's ideal gains a case where it is kept by a householder's widow with an unfinished duty, showing it need not mean withdrawal from affairs

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised as Kantukkatan's son
Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage
Civakan's companions, who have come to the hermitage in search of him
the women ascetics of the hermitage who sheltered Vijayai
the god who carried Civakan from the execution ground (named only as a deity here)
the merchant who took up and raised Civakan (mentioned)
the usurper king, called கீழ்மகன் here (mentioned)

source_issues: Most stanzas from 1799 on were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful (1802 line 3, 1804 line 1, 1807 line 2, 1811 lines 1-2, 1813 lines 2-3).
1798 line 4 ends with a stray full stop (வீழ்ந்தாள்.).
1812 line 3 சோந்தனந் looks like a misprint for சேர்ந்தனம்.
1816 line 3 செந் நில்லலா divides doubtfully (perhaps செந்நில்லா).
